script.opening: "I’ve always been really bendy — double-jointed — but now my joints keep partly dislocating and aching all the time, I bruise at the slightest thing, my skin’s soft and stretchy, and I’m shattered. I get dizzy standing up too. Someone said it could be Ehlers-Danlos. I’ve been fobbed off a lot. What is it?"

facts.text: Always "bendy" — did gymnastics as a child. Over the last 3 years: shoulders and kneecaps partly dislocate several times a month, usually go back by themselves. Aching joints daily, worse after activity.

Can put both palms flat on the floor with knees straight, bend both little fingers back past 90 degrees, touch both thumbs to her forearms, and her elbows bend backwards. Knees bend backwards too. (A Beighton score of 9 out of 9.)
Bruises easily; skin soft and "a bit stretchy", not see-through. Scars heal normally, not wide or paper-thin.

Dizzy and heart racing when she stands, especially in the morning and in hot showers. Never fully fainted. If asked: practice nurse did a standing test last week — "my pulse went up by about 35 and my blood pressure stayed the same".
No family members with sudden early death, burst blood vessels or bowel rupture. No collapsed lung. Not unusually tall, no lens problems. No severe sudden tummy or chest pain.

IBS-like tummy symptoms. Heavy periods. Tired all the time. Mood: "being told it’s nothing gets me down" — no self-harm. Mum is also bendy. No medicines except ibuprofen sometimes. No allergies. Works part-time as a barista.
Guarded at first, expecting to be fobbed off. Warm up if the doctor listens and believes you. Ask: "So it’s real?" and "Will physio actually help?" The pain and tiredness matter most.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — not being believed; she has been told "it’s anxiety" twice and is close to giving up. Worried whether she can ever work full time.
ice.expectations: "Someone to recognise it and actually help."

cues: "I’ve been fobbed off a lot" — needs validation.
"I get dizzy standing up" — possible PoTS to explore.
"My mum is bendy too" (if family history is asked) — inherited pattern; check for serious-subtype red flags.

checkpoints.text: Recognises HYPERMOBILITY SPECTRUM DISORDER / hypermobile EDS (generalised hypermobility, recurrent pain/dislocations, soft skin/easy bruising) and assesses hypermobility (Beighton score, 5 or more), knowing hEDS is a clinical diagnosis with no genetic test, taking it seriously rather than dismissing

Recognises the MULTISYSTEM picture/comorbidities — chronic pain, fatigue, PoTS/autonomic dysfunction (lying and standing pulse/BP), GI dysmotility, anxiety/depression, poor healing — and checks FBC and clotting for the bruising

Is alert to RED FLAGS for rare serious EDS subtypes (vascular EDS — arterial/organ rupture, family history of arterial events/sudden death; classical EDS — very stretchy skin with atrophic scars; marfanoid/aortic features) needing genetics referral

Manages HOLISTICALLY — physiotherapy (joint stabilisation, graded strengthening, proprioception, pacing), chronic-pain approach (no opioids for chronic primary pain, NICE NG193), and management of associated PoTS/GI/mood, with work support (Equality Act 2010)
Makes or supports the diagnosis in primary care and refers appropriately (rheumatology/hypermobility service/MDT where pathways allow; clinical genetics if a serious subtype suspected)
VALIDATES the experience and the sense of being repeatedly dismissed, and checks understanding of the holistic plan
Explores how the condition and years of not being believed have affected her daily life and mood, and agrees a realistic, prioritised plan she feels ownership of
Safety-nets and follows up: serious-subtype red flags warranting urgent/specialist review, physiotherapy/pain/PoTS management, referral, and review — recognition + holistic management, not dismissal

worked.txt: "I’m sorry you’ve been fobbed off — what you’re describing is real. Being very flexible with joints that dislocate and ache, soft stretchy skin, easy bruising and fatigue fits a hypermobility condition, possibly hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos. Let me assess your flexibility properly with a scoring system. There’s no blood or genetic test for the hypermobile type — it’s diagnosed with a set of clinical criteria."
"This often affects more than joints — the dizziness on standing, tummy symptoms, fatigue and mood can all be part of it. So we look at the whole picture, not just one joint."

"A couple of safety questions — any family history of arteries or organs rupturing, or sudden young deaths? Very thin, see-through skin, or wide stretched scars? … No. Those would point to a rarer, more serious type needing genetics, which doesn’t seem to fit you. I’ll still check a blood count and clotting because of the bruising."

"The cornerstone is physiotherapy — strengthening and stabilising the joints and improving control — plus pacing to avoid flares. We’ll manage the pain sensibly (simple painkillers and other approaches rather than strong opioids), check your pulse and blood pressure lying and standing, and tackle the dizziness with fluids, salt, standing slowly and compression, and your mood and tummy symptoms too."

"I’ll refer you to the rheumatology or hypermobility service if our local pathway allows, to coordinate care, and to genetics if anything suggests a serious subtype. If work is affected, this can count as a disability under the Equality Act, so adjustments can be made. You deserve a proper, joined-up approach."
"Come back if joints dislocate frequently or you can’t manage the pain, and urgently for any severe sudden abdominal/chest pain. We’ll build a plan around you."

f.learning: Generalised JOINT HYPERMOBILITY with recurrent joint pain, subluxations/dislocations, soft/stretchy skin, easy bruising, poor wound healing, fatigue and often autonomic (dizziness/palpitations) and GI symptoms suggests a HYPERMOBILITY SPECTRUM DISORDER / hypermobile EHLERS-DANLOS SYNDROME (hEDS) — assessed for hypermobility with the BEIGHTON score (5 or more between puberty and 50 in the 2017 criteria, international); there is no genetic test for hEDS, which is a clinical diagnosis the GP can often make, and marked skin stretch with atrophic scars points instead to classical EDS. It is often under-recognised and patients are frequently dismissed, so take it seriously and recognise the MULTISYSTEM picture and comorbidities (chronic pain, fatigue, PoTS/autonomic dysfunction — a sustained rise of 30 beats per minute or more within 10 minutes of standing, checked with a lying-to-standing test — GI dysmotility, anxiety/depression, easy bruising needing FBC and a clotting screen, poor healing). Be alert to RED FLAGS suggesting rare but SERIOUS EDS subtypes needing specialist/genetics referral — in particular VASCULAR EDS (risk of arterial, bowel or uterine rupture; thin translucent skin, easy bruising, a family history of arterial events/sudden death) and marfanoid/aortic features — which substantially change risk and management. Manage holistically: validate the experience; physiotherapy is the cornerstone (joint stabilisation, graded strengthening, proprioception, pacing to avoid deconditioning); use a chronic-pain approach (simple analgesia; NICE NG193 advises against starting opioids for chronic primary pain; pacing, psychological support); and manage associated PoTS (fluids/salt/compression), GI symptoms and mood, with lifestyle and occupational support (the condition may be a disability under the Equality Act 2010). Refer appropriately — rheumatology/hypermobility service for MDT care where pathways allow, and clinical genetics if a serious subtype is suspected — avoiding the common pitfall of dismissing the patient.

knowledge.guideline: [1] International Classification of the Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes and hEDS diagnostic criteria (Malfait et al., 2017) (international) · [2] Beighton score, as used in the 2017 criteria (international) · [3] Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus on postural tachycardia syndrome (2015) (international) · [4] NICE NG193 (chronic pain in over 16s, 2021) · [5] Equality Act 2010
knowledge.summary: Generalised joint hypermobility with recurrent pain and subluxations, soft skin, easy bruising, fatigue and dizziness on standing suggests hypermobility spectrum disorder or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. There is no genetic test for hEDS; it is a clinical diagnosis using the 2017 criteria. Look for features of rarer types, especially vascular EDS, which need clinical genetics. Management is holistic and led by physiotherapy, with a careful approach to pain and attention to dizziness, fatigue and mood. Take her seriously.

points.t: The Beighton score (0–9) records passive little-finger extension, thumb to forearm, elbow and knee hyperextension beyond 10°, and palms flat on the floor [2]. In the 2017 hEDS criteria, a score of 5 or more counts as generalised hypermobility between puberty and age 50 [1]. A lower score with a convincing history can still be hypermobility.

hEDS needs generalised hypermobility plus systemic features, family history or musculoskeletal complications, and exclusion of other conditions [1]. People who do not meet all criteria have hypermobility spectrum disorder, which can be just as disabling and is managed the same way.

Thin, translucent skin, extensive bruising, arterial dissection or aneurysm, bowel or uterine rupture, or a family history of sudden early death suggest vascular EDS. Very stretchy skin with wide atrophic scars suggests classical EDS. A tall, marfanoid build, lens dislocation or aortic root dilatation suggest Marfan syndrome or a related condition. These need clinical genetics referral [1].

Chronic pain, fatigue, dizziness from postural tachycardia, gut dysmotility, bladder symptoms, anxiety and low mood are common. Postural tachycardia syndrome in adults is a sustained heart-rate rise of 30 beats per minute or more within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotension [3]; a lying-to-standing test in surgery is a reasonable first step.
No blood test confirms hEDS. With easy bruising, check FBC and a clotting screen; with fatigue, consider FBC, ferritin, TFTs and coeliac serology. An ECG is reasonable with palpitations or dizziness.

Physiotherapy is central: graded strengthening, joint stability and proprioception, with pacing. Occupational therapy helps with daily activities and joint protection. For pain, use simple analgesia and non-drug approaches. NICE NG193 [4] advises against starting opioids for chronic primary pain, and opioids are best avoided for long-term hypermobility pain. For postural symptoms, advise fluids, salt as appropriate, slow standing and compression garments. Support mood and fatigue.

The GP can often make the diagnosis. Refer to rheumatology or a hypermobility service where local pathways allow, and to clinical genetics if a rarer type is suspected. The condition may be a disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5], which supports workplace adjustments.

model.text: Hello Ms Carter, I’m Dr Patel. What would you like to talk about?

I’ve always been really bendy, double-jointed, but now my joints keep partly dislocating and aching all the time. I bruise at the slightest thing, my skin’s soft and stretchy, and I’m shattered. I get dizzy standing up too. Someone said it could be Ehlers-Danlos. I’ve been fobbed off a lot. What is it?

I’m sorry you’ve felt fobbed off. What you’re describing is real, and I want to understand it properly. I’ll ask about each part, ask you to show me a few movements on the camera, and then tell you what I think and what we can do. Is that okay?
Yes. Thank you.
Which joints dislocate, how often, and do they go back by themselves?
Different joints, quite often. They usually go back on their own.
Tell me about the dizziness. Does it happen when you stand up, with a racing heart, and have you ever fainted?
Yes, when I stand up. My heart goes fast and I feel faint.
Any problems with your tummy or bowels, or your bladder?
Sometimes, yes.
When you cut yourself, how does it heal? Is your skin very thin, so you can see the veins easily?
model.why: Skin features of classical and vascular EDS

model.text: It’s soft, but I wouldn’t say see-through.
Has anyone in the family had a burst artery or bowel, or died suddenly at a young age?
No, not that I know of.
How is all this affecting your life day to day, and your mood?
I’m exhausted, and being told it’s nothing gets me down.
What do you think is going on?
I think it might be Ehlers-Danlos.
And what worries you most, and what are you hoping for today?
Not being believed. I want someone to recognise it and actually help.

I’ll talk you through a standard flexibility test on the camera, and look at your skin and any scars. The nurse’s lying and standing pulse and blood pressure are in your notes, and I’ll arrange for someone to listen to your heart.
model.why: Beighton score, skin, marfanoid features, active stand test

model.text: Okay.

Your symptoms fit a hypermobility condition. It’s either hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or a closely related condition called hypermobility spectrum disorder. There’s no blood test for it; it’s diagnosed with a set of clinical criteria, and I’ll go through those with you. Both are managed the same way.
model.why: Names HSD or hEDS and explains clinical diagnosis

model.text: So it’s real.
It’s real. The dizziness and fast heart on standing may be part of it too, something called postural tachycardia. The checks I’ve done will help with that.
model.why: Affirms and links the multisystem features

model.text: I’d like to check some bloods because of the bruising and tiredness, including a blood count and clotting. The mainstay of treatment is physiotherapy with someone who understands hypermobility, working on strength and joint control, and pacing so you don’t boom and bust.
Will physio actually help?

It can, if it’s the right kind. Specialist hypermobility physio is different from general exercises, and it’s gradual. For the pain, we’ll use simple painkillers and other approaches rather than strong opioids, which tend to cause more problems long term. For the dizziness, plenty of fluids, standing slowly and compression tights can help.
model.why: Pain approach avoiding opioids; postural measures

model.text: Okay. Do I need a specialist?

I’ll refer you to the rheumatology or hypermobility service if our local pathway allows. If anything suggested a rarer, more serious type, I’d refer to genetics, but nothing you’ve told me points that way. Which of these matters most to you to start with?
model.why: Appropriate referral and prioritisation with her

model.text: The pain and the tiredness.

Then we’ll start there. If you ever have sudden severe pain in your chest, tummy or head, or you faint and injure yourself, get urgent help. A joint that won’t go back needs A&E. Let’s review in four weeks with the results. Can you tell me the plan?
Bloods, specialist physio, fluids and slow standing, simple painkillers, referral. Urgent help for sudden severe pain or a joint that won’t go back.
That’s it. We’ll build on it together.

social.t: Fatigue and pain may affect work or study. Discuss reasonable adjustments and a fit note where needed.
If daily living or mobility is significantly affected, she may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment.

legal.t: A long-term condition with a substantial effect on daily activities can count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work or college.
If she has fainted or nearly fainted, discuss whether it is safe to drive and check DVLA guidance on syncope.

professional.t: Being repeatedly disbelieved damages trust and delays care. Listening, recording her account and acting on it is part of good practice (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: UK charities for Ehlers-Danlos and hypermobility provide information, peer support and physiotherapy resources; also PoTS UK for postural tachycardia.

redFlags: Thin translucent skin, arterial or organ rupture, family history of sudden early death: vascular EDS, genetics
Marfanoid build, lens or aortic problems: genetics or cardiology
Syncope with injury or exertional syncope: cardiac assessment
Joint that will not reduce: A&E

playbook.diagnosis: Hypermobility spectrum disorder or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (2017 criteria), with possible postural tachycardia syndrome; no features of vascular or classical EDS on history.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your connective tissue, which holds your joints and skin together, is more stretchy than usual. That’s why your joints slip and ache, you bruise easily and you may feel dizzy on standing. It’s real, and it can be managed.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve felt fobbed off, and you wondered about Ehlers-Danlos. I think you’re right that this is a hypermobility condition, and we’ll work on it together.”
management.psychosocial: Validation; mood support; work or study adjustments; PIP if eligible.
sharedPlan: FBC and clotting screen; ferritin, TFTs and coeliac serology for fatigue
Specialist hypermobility physiotherapy and pacing; occupational therapy
Simple analgesia and non-drug approaches; avoid opioids
Fluids, slow standing and compression for postural symptoms
Rheumatology or hypermobility service where available; genetics if red flags
safetyNet: Sudden severe chest, abdominal or head pain: 999
Joint that will not go back: A&E

pitfalls.intro: The failing candidate dismisses her or hands over a leaflet. The passing candidate recognises the condition, screens for the dangerous types and builds a practical plan with her.

items.why: The Beighton score underpins the diagnosis.
items.fix: Do or describe the Beighton score.

items.why: Vascular EDS carries a risk of arterial and organ rupture.
items.fix: Ask about skin, rupture and family sudden deaths; refer to genetics if present.

items.why: Postural tachycardia is common and treatable.
items.fix: Lying and standing pulse and BP; advise fluids and compression.

items.why: She has been fobbed off before.
items.fix: Validate and confirm it is real.

items.fail: Overloading her with everything at once.
items.fix: Ask what matters most and plan a review.

wordPics.fail: Dismisses it as ‘just being flexible’, or orders a genetic test for hEDS; no vascular red-flag screen; opioids for pain.
wordPics.pass: Recognises HSD or hEDS, uses the Beighton score, screens for vascular EDS, and plans physiotherapy-led care.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: validates her experience, explains there is no genetic test for hEDS, recognises postural tachycardia, checks bruising bloods, avoids opioids, and agrees priorities with her.

avoid.dont: “Lots of people are flexible. It’s nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “What you’re describing is real, and it has a name.”
avoid.why: Repeats the dismissal she has experienced.

avoid.dont: “We’ll do a gene test to confirm it.”
avoid.instead: “There’s no gene test for hypermobile EDS; it’s diagnosed clinically.”
avoid.why: No gene has been identified for hEDS (2017 criteria).

avoid.dont: “Let’s try something stronger, like codeine or tramadol.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s focus on physio, pacing and simple painkillers.”
avoid.why: Long-term opioids cause harm without clear benefit in chronic pain.

Postural tachycardia syndrome in adults is a sustained heart-rate rise of 30 beats per minute or more within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotension [3]; a lying-to-standing test in surgery is a reasonable first step.
No blood test confirms hEDS. With easy bruising, check FBC and a clotting screen; with fatigue, consider FBC, ferritin, TFTs and coeliac serology. An ECG is reasonable with palpitations or dizziness.

Physiotherapy is central: graded strengthening, joint stability and proprioception, with pacing. Occupational therapy helps with daily activities and joint protection. For pain, use simple analgesia and non-drug approaches. NICE NG193 [4] advises against starting opioids for chronic primary pain, and opioids are best avoided for long-term hypermobility pain. For postural symptoms, advise fluids, salt as appropriate, slow standing and compression garments. Support mood and fatigue.

The GP can often make the diagnosis. Refer to rheumatology or a hypermobility service where local pathways allow, and to clinical genetics if a rarer type is suspected. The condition may be a disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5], which supports workplace adjustments.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged being fobbed off before narrowing.
Explored the effect on daily life, exhaustion and mood from not being believed.
Picked up recurrent subluxations, skin features, bruising and postural dizziness with palpitations.
Idea: Ehlers-Danlos. Concern: not being believed. Expectation: recognition and real help.
Beighton score, skin and scars, marfanoid features, heart, lying and standing pulse and BP; FBC, clotting, and fatigue bloods.
hEDS versus HSD versus classical or vascular EDS and Marfan; bleeding disorder for bruising; PoTS.
Screened vascular EDS red flags: thin skin, family history of rupture or sudden early death.
Hypermobility spectrum disorder or hEDS, with possible postural tachycardia.
Hypermobility physiotherapy, pacing, non-opioid pain approach, fluids and compression for dizziness; priorities agreed.
Addressed mood and fatigue; rheumatology or hypermobility service; genetics only if red flags.

social.t: Fatigue and pain may affect work or study. Discuss reasonable adjustments and a fit note where needed.
If daily living or mobility is significantly affected, she may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment.

legal.t: A long-term condition with a substantial effect on daily activities can count as a disability, giving a right to reasonable adjustments at work or college.
If she has fainted or nearly fainted, discuss whether it is safe to drive and check DVLA guidance on syncope.

professional.t: Being repeatedly disbelieved damages trust and delays care. Listening, recording her account and acting on it is part of good practice (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: UK charities for Ehlers-Danlos and hypermobility provide information, peer support and physiotherapy resources; also PoTS UK for postural tachycardia.

redFlags: Thin translucent skin, arterial or organ rupture, family history of sudden early death: vascular EDS, genetics
Marfanoid build, lens or aortic problems: genetics or cardiology
Syncope with injury or exertional syncope: cardiac assessment
Joint that will not reduce: A&E

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Hypermobility spectrum disorder or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (2017 criteria), with possible postural tachycardia syndrome; no features of vascular or classical EDS on history.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your connective tissue, which holds your joints and skin together, is more stretchy than usual. That’s why your joints slip and ache, you bruise easily and you may feel dizzy on standing. It’s real, and it can be managed.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve felt fobbed off, and you wondered about Ehlers-Danlos. I think you’re right that this is a hypermobility condition, and we’ll work on it together.”
management.psychosocial: Validation; mood support; work or study adjustments; PIP if eligible.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The failing candidate dismisses her or hands over a leaflet. The passing candidate recognises the condition, screens for the dangerous types and builds a practical plan with her.

items.why: The Beighton score underpins the diagnosis.
items.fix: Do or describe the Beighton score.

items.why: Vascular EDS carries a risk of arterial and organ rupture.
items.fix: Ask about skin, rupture and family sudden deaths; refer to genetics if present.

items.why: Postural tachycardia is common and treatable.
items.fix: Lying and standing pulse and BP; advise fluids and compression.

items.why: She has been fobbed off before.
items.fix: Validate and confirm it is real.

items.fail: Overloading her with everything at once.
items.fix: Ask what matters most and plan a review.
